blocks.text: Now that we have dealt fully with smoke, it remains for us to speak of the bravery of bees, with reference to those passages of Scripture in which the most hostile enemies are compared with bees: as above, the Amorites, of whom Moses says, And they pursued you, as bees do. And in Psal. CXVIII, 12. David says of his enemies, They surrounded me like bees. And in Es. VII, 18. The Lord will hiss for the bee that is in the land of Assur. There the Chaldee has: The Lord will call to the mighty forces, דאנון תקיפין כדבריתא, which are strong like bees, and he will bring them from the borders of the land of Assyria. And in the same place R. Selomo, [III, 364] לדבורה חיל גבורים דעוקצים כדבורים, To the bee, that is, to an army of mighty men who sting like bees. Lest these comparisons should seem to fall below the dignity of the subject, it must be understood that the bee has a great spirit in so slight a little body; and that, to protect their honey, bees do not fear to attack with their hostile stings not only men but even all the largest animals, and sometimes they kill them. Aristotle, History, book 9, ch. 40: Κτείνουσι δὲ βάλλουσαι καὶ τὰ μεγάλα τῶν ζώων. καὶ ἵππος ἤδη ἀπέθανεν ὑπὸ μελιττῶν [Kteinousi de ballousai kai ta megala tōn zōōn. kai hippos ēdē apethanen hypo melittōn]. By driving in their sting they kill all the largest animals. Indeed, a horse once died from being stung by bees. Hence Pliny, book 11, ch. 18: There are instances of horses killed by them. Moreover, Aelian, book 17, ch. 35, reports from Antenor that the Rhaucians, a people of Crete, were driven out of their city by the stings of χαλκοειδῶν [chalkoeidōn] bees and migrated elsewhere. It is no wonder, then, if the same creatures proved fatal to Hermonax, a boy, of whom Antipater writes in book 1 of the Anthology, ch. 37:
Τὸ βρέφος Ἑρμάνακτα διεχρήσασθε μέλισσαι, [To brephos Hermanakta diechrēsasthe melissai,]
Κοῦρον ἀποπλανίην, ἐπιμάζιον, Ἑρμώνακτα Φεῦ! βρέφος ὡς ἀδίκως εἵλετε βουγενέες; [Kouron apoplaniēn, epimazion, Hermōnakta / Pheu! brephos hōs adikōs heilete bougenees?]
The wandering, suckling boy Hermonax, an infant, alas! how unjustly you destroyed him, bees! Accordingly, in Theocritus, Idyll 19, Cupid the κηριοκλέπτης [kēriokleptēs] complains to his mother
— — — — ὅττι γε τυτθὸν [col. 510] Θηρίον ἐντὶ μέλισσα, καὶ ἁλίκα τραύματα ποιεῖ· [— — — — hotti ge tytthon / Thērion enti melissa, kai halika traumata poiei;]

That though the bee is so tiny a little creature, it inflicts such great wounds. Swarms of bees have also often been of use in war. Thus in Appian's Mithridatic Wars, when the troops of Lucullus were attacking Themiscyra through tunnels, the Themiscyrans sent bears and other wild beasts, and σμήνη μελισσῶν [smēnē melissōn], swarms of bees, against the workmen. And when Amurath was besieging Alba Graeca, the townspeople defended themselves by letting loose swarms of bees on the Turks, as Bonfinius writes in Decade 3, book 4. Not unlike this is what Widukind reports in book 1 of On the Deeds of the Saxons: one of the commanders of the Emperor Henry, besieged by Giselbert, king of Lotharingia, held back the attackers by throwing beehives at them; the horses, driven to frenzy by the stings, either threw their riders or made them useless for fighting. And in the year 1513, when Barriga, a Portuguese commander, had reduced Tanli, a town of the Moors in the territory of Xiatima, almost to the last extremity, the townspeople, seeing themselves brought into the utmost danger, set on fire countless beehives, of which they had great plenty, and let them down from the walls. Our men, both scorched by the flames of the hives and goaded by the stings of the bees, were forced to abandon the assault. These are the words of Osorius, book 8, On the Deeds of Emmanuel. Therefore, if not true, [III, 365] it is at least plausible, what Iamblichus writes in Photius about the forces besieging Rhodanes and Sinonis: Φεύγουσιν ὁ στρατὸς, τῷ τῶν μελισσῶν πολέμῳ πονούμενοι [Pheugousin ho stratos, tō tōn melissōn polemō ponoumenoi]. The forces flee, distressed by the attack of the bees ^{(5)}. Nor is it altogether incredible, what we cited above from Herodotus, that certain regions beyond the Ister were inaccessible to men because of the multitude of bees. Today, among the penalties that the Jewish nation imposes on an adulterer, one is that he must pass naked in summer through a dense crowd of bees and expose his body to their stings until he is swollen all over; and after he has recovered, he must undergo the same penalty again, or even more often, according to the gravity of the sin. So it is stated in ch. 34 of Buxtorf's Synagoga.
